texts: Day 1 — Across the equator to a tropical island nation

The starting point of this trip was Chubu Centrair International Airport. We flew Cathay Pacific via Hong Kong to Jakarta, the capital of Indonesia. Leaving behind KEN, who would join us a week later, the two of us, having just finished presenting our graduation theses, boarded the plane in high spirits...
But soon after boarding, Ooi realised his wallet was missing. He had split his money into two wallets, so he didn't lose everything, but it was an inauspicious start.

We arrived at Hong Kong International Airport. Like the dull, cloudy sky, Ooi's mood didn't clear. After all, he had lost 50,000 yen before even leaving the country. Hong Kong airport is simply huge. Just walking was quite a distance. And unexpectedly, the land around it wasn't flat but mountainous. We had about three hours until the next flight. By then we wanted some information about the lost wallet. To look up Centrair's phone number, we decided to use an internet terminal near a kiosk. You could use it if you bought something at the kiosk. Ooi bought an éclair. He paid in US dollars, so he got a little change back in Hong Kong dollars. They'll probably never be used. When we contacted Centrair, it turned out the wallet had been handed in to the police! We forgot to check what was inside, but praying it was all there, we continued our journey. Ooi's face was beaming.

Across the equator into the southern hemisphere. In Indonesia we would first enjoy diving on Lombok, then meet up with KEN. By rental car we were aiming for the equator on Sumatra, to the west of here.

Arrived in Jakarta! The arrivals lobby of Soekarno–Hatta International Airport didn't feel much like an airport; it was more like a station. After getting a visa ($25) and clearing immigration, we changed money into Indonesian rupiah. The rate was about 100 rupiah to the yen.

After changing money, as we headed outside, taxi drivers kept calling out, "Hey! Taxi, taxi!" The touting was intense. And though it was around 9 p.m., there were incredible numbers of people. Watching out for pickpockets, we looked for a rental car company to make arranging a car later go smoothly. A man from a rental company who called out to us led us outside the airport. Instantly, warm, muggy air wrapped around us. Hot...

The rental company man showed us lots of the rental cars lined up outside the airport. The mainstream model was a Toyota minivan called the Kijang. It isn't made in Japan, but it's about the size of a Voxy. When we asked the price, he said about 5,000 yen a day. That's about twice the price in our guidebook. Had prices gone up, or were we being ripped off? To have to negotiate like this as soon as we arrived... Very tiring. It was late anyway, so we stopped looking for a car at the airport and decided to look in the city tomorrow.

From the airport to central Jakarta we skimped and took a bus rather than a taxi. A fairly comfortable bus called DAMRI runs from the airport to the city for about 200 yen one way. Given that it uses the expressway and the distance, in Japan it would easily be over 1,000 yen; we were already feeling how cheap things were.

After getting off at the last stop, Gambir Station, we went to the Jalan Jaksa area, where cheap lodgings are said to cluster. First things first: securing a bed, so we looked for a hotel. We dashed into Borneo Hostel and asked, and they said there was just one room left. It had air conditioning, so it was the most expensive room (about 750 yen each).
After resting a little in the room, we got peckish and went to a nearby food stall. Even though it was around 11 at night, this street was very lively.

Our memorable first dish in Indonesia was the classic nasi goreng, in other words fried rice. About 70 yen a plate. The snack-like thing is krupuk, a prawn cracker, said to be essential with nasi goreng. Crispy and pretty tasty. As expected, the nasi goreng was quite spicy (the writer has a sweet tooth). While we were eating, a middle-aged woman and man started talking to us. English got through reasonably well, so the conversation livened up. Then suddenly they started shouting a filthy Japanese word! They must have learned it from other Japanese tourists.
To the next day
Day 2 — To Lombok on Batavia Air

Jakarta is in the tropics, so the temperature hardly changes through the year, averaging about 30 °C. The year is divided into a dry season and a rainy season, and March is supposedly near the end of the rainy season. Maybe because of that, it was too humid to sleep well. On top of that, the air conditioning didn't work well, even though the remote said it was set to 18 °C.

I didn't sleep much, but bathing (mandi) in the morning was refreshing. Cheap lodgings in Indonesia usually have no bathtub. Some apparently don't even have a shower, but last night's place had a cold shower. If there's no shower, you scoop water from a tank next to the toilet with a dipper and pour it over yourself. Whether shower or tank, pouring water over yourself is called mandi, and Indonesians apparently mandi several times a day. Having tried it, I understood: mandi feels wonderful. In the heat your body inevitably gets sticky, but after a mandi you stay fresh for a while ♪ We left the hostel and went out to find a money changer and someone who would rent us a car. Again, drivers of taxis and bajaj (three-wheelers) kept calling out to us. There were lots of stray cats and stray chickens in town.

Wandering around Jalan Jaksa. The roads were overflowing with motorbikes. The red vehicle in the middle of the photo is a bajaj. We never used one on this trip, but it's a kind of semi-taxi, apparently a little cheaper than a taxi.

On the way, liver skewers were on sale for about 10 yen, so we tried some, but they weren't to our taste. There was a neat little diner, so we went in and ordered the mie ayam set. 145 yen including soup and a drink: cheap. Mie ayam looks like ramen without the soup. In the mouth, the chicken flavour comes through nicely; very tasty. Reasonably priced too, so nothing to complain about. We tried several rental car companies, but none would rent to us. Thinking we would have to rent at the airport after all, we went looking for a money changer instead. We had only changed about 2,000 yen at the airport, so even a slightly better rate would help.

As we walked, a sudden squall! We fled into a nearby clothes shop. In the shoe section we came across the strange sight of mannequins displaying only their lower halves, upside down. The rain didn't stop. We saw a boy nearby with an umbrella calling out to passers-by, and thinking he was selling umbrellas, we called him over, gave him money, took an umbrella and set off together. Then the boy followed us, getting soaked by the rain. It seemed he hadn't sold it but was only lending it. He followed us getting drenched, and we felt very guilty. We gave the umbrella back at the bank and said goodbye. The rate at the airport was a little better than at the bank, so we had no more business in the centre. In the rain we put on raincoats and went back to the bus terminal. What we noticed: we got less wet than with the umbrella.

Having found the rate was better at the airport, we first changed money in the international arrivals lobby and then set about arranging a rental car. The negotiations were extremely difficult. First, the rental period was long, about two weeks, and we wouldn't only be driving on Java, where Jakarta is. When we said we would take the ferry to Sumatra, the rental company staff started making a fuss as if that was out of the question. On top of that, they quoted about 6,000 yen a day. We explained in detail where we would drive and kept negotiating for a long time, and in the end they gave way and we reached an agreement. Promising to call their mobile when we came back to Jakarta from Lombok, we parted from them, looking forward to a great adventure in the car. At this point we had no way of knowing about all the trouble this rental car would bring. We moved to the domestic terminal by shuttle bus. It felt like a slightly simpler version of the international terminal, and of course it was packed with locals.

We went to A&W for lunch. There wasn't a single McDonald's at the airport, but there were A&Ws everywhere. It brought back memories of eating at one in Canada. It was surprising that the set menus included rice. McDonald's in Japan has nothing like a rice menu. They must really love rice.

The domestic departure lounge had an atmospheric design, and the walkways just had roofs, a very open feel. There was a courtyard too, and lots of people sitting on the ground, which felt very Indonesian. After this, the announcement for the Batavia Air flight we were to take just wouldn't come. In the end: delayed 30 minutes, then another 30 minutes, then another hour... It ended up two hours late. While we waited, bread was handed out, as if to placate us. Boxed meals were handed out too, but apparently for passengers on another flight. How long must they have been kept waiting? Strangely, none of the people in the waiting room seemed irritated; it was as if this was normal.
From the waiting room we went to the plane by bus. This bus seems to have once been in service in Japan.

Aboard Batavia Air at last! But it was incredibly hot and humid! Was the air conditioning broken? After take-off it got a little cooler, but delays and dodgy air conditioning: is this Batavia quality? Via Surabaya, we landed at the airport at Mataram on Lombok. It was dark so we couldn't really tell, but it was a very basic airport, and on leaving the plane the passengers just walked briskly off in one direction. From Mataram we took a taxi to Raja's Bungalows in Senggigi, which we had booked in advance. Another tiring day of nothing but travel.
To the next day
Day 3 — Paradise = Gili Trawangan
This is what our room looked like. It had a mosquito net, and a fan on the ceiling. Unlike Jakarta it wasn't very humid, and we slept soundly.
This place had a shower too. There was no ceiling; you could see the sky, very open.

Breakfast time in a nearby annex. The so-called Lombok coffee they served looked like powder put in a cup with hot water poured straight on, but if you drink only the top it's very mild and delicious.

In front of the Dream Divers office in the town of Senggigi. This is the dive shop that would look after us as we worked toward our PADI Open Water Diver licence. When we said hello, we learned that the dive shop people had come to meet us at the airport yesterday. The two-hour flight delay was one reason, but we had been told to go to the hotel by taxi, so it seems the message hadn't got through properly.

To get from Senggigi to our destination, Gili Trawangan, you first go by van to a remote port called Bangsal. Lombok's coastline is very rugged, a twisting route full of ups and downs. After driving for a while, small islands appeared offshore. There are no islands further west, so this had to be our destination, Gili Trawangan, said to be a backpacker's paradise.

From Bangsal we switched to a small boat and went by sea to Trawangan. Just as on the map, you can see the three islands of Gili Air, Meno and Trawangan side by side. By the way, gili apparently means "small island" in the language of the Sasak people who live on Lombok. Trawangan is the largest of the three Gili islands off north-west Lombok, and rises a little in the middle. They say the Japanese army once had a lookout over the Lombok Strait on this hill, and an air-raid shelter still remains.

When we reached the island, the Dream Divers office was right there. After arriving, we started by looking for somewhere to stay. They recommended the bungalows attached to the office, but they were a bit pricey, so when we said we'd like somewhere a little cheaper, office staff took us to several places. Once our lodging was settled, the lessons toward our licence started straight away. First we watched a DVD for about an hour to learn the basics of diving. After that, straight into practice in the pool in front of the office. Our instructor was a slightly funky guy with tattoos, or so we thought; when we later asked his age, he was 37, which was a surprise.

After the pool session we went for lunch. The street in front of the dive shop is the island's main street, lined with many shops. There are lots of Westerners on this island, and nearly all the restaurants are bar-style places they'd like. We didn't see anyone who looked Japanese at all. We went into a café and ordered pasta. While we waited, two boys who called themselves Roshi and Ena started talking to us. As we enjoyed some small talk, they began suggesting we try a delicious mushroom juice. "Delicious, cheap," they pushed hard, so we ordered just one glass. They pushed hard for two, but we declined. This was our biggest mistake on this island. When we paid after the meal we were stunned to be charged about 2,000 yen, not a huge amount, but it should have been about 600. We protested it was too expensive, but "Happy Drink" had been slyly written in a corner of the blackboard. We grudgingly paid, but in fact the juice we had been made to drink contained magic mushrooms, a type of drug. They have been illegal in Japan since 2002. They're known too because a famous actor once suffered poisoning symptoms from them. On top of these mushrooms, people on this island casually try to sell you marijuana. Their stock phrase is "Happa happa!" We would later learn that many tourists who carelessly got involved have been arrested, and I thought we absolutely had to be careful about this. It felt like the island's baptism, and it made me very angry, but I vowed that from now on we would never accept their offers and would be much more on guard.

After lunch, the open-water training already. We loaded the gear onto the dive boat and set out to sea. The breeze felt great. The Open Water Diver course has four open-water dives in total, and the first two go to 12 m. Our first dive site was Bounty. On "3, 2, 1" we dived into the sea. Breathing from the regulator, we gradually descended toward the seabed. The clear, beautiful water was about 30 °C and very comfortable. It felt like we could stay down for hours. As we approached the seabed, a stunning view spread out: coral reefs and countless tropical fish. Their beauty, and how moved we were, can't be put into words. The advertising line that you'll meet far more creatures diving into the sea for 10 minutes than hiking a mountain for an hour made sense.

The dive at Bounty was about 12 m deep, and we were hardly tired at all. But because of the big change in pressure, our ears felt quite strange afterwards. Ooi couldn't equalise (clear his ears) properly, so he had been enduring a lot. We went back to our lodging, Dessy Bungalows, for a while. But the power seemed to be off. On this tropical island, not being able to use a fan is really tough. On top of that, we couldn't charge our phones or cameras. "They've cut the power because we chose a cheap place!" we fumed, but we later learned that on the Gilis the power supply is unstable and outages are frequent. It was clearly written in the lodging's leaflet too. Of course, restaurants and fairly upmarket hotels seem to have their own generators.

After a rest at the lodging, we went out to explore the island. It's only a little over 2 km from north to south, so it should be perfect for a walk. This is the island's main street, lined with many bar-style restaurants.

We walked south along the main street. Most of the road is unpaved. The island has a rule that no motorised vehicles are allowed, so there are no cars or motorbikes. The main means of transport are horse carts (cidomo) and bicycles.

Going inland, there were local people's houses and empty plots, with lots of chickens and goats roaming free. Watching the chickens, you really start to think they aren't very bright. They roam free, but they aren't pets; they must be for meat or eggs, yet the chickens seem to think about nothing all day but pecking the ground for food. If one of their friends disappears one day, they don't care. Even if a friend is slaughtered in front of them, there's no particular fuss. If there's food in front of the house, they don't run away either.

We were walking inland but lost track of where we were, so we walked on at random and came out on the coast near the southern tip of the island. We followed the coast north for a while and reached the west side of the island. While the east side bustles with shops, the west side has hardly any shops, or even houses. A calm shore with almost no waves, and in the distance you can see Bali too.

The island was bigger than we expected and we got tired. Walking was a bother, so we hopped on a passing horse cart. Back on the east side of the island, we went to a bar restaurant. Prices on this island are a bit high: a pizza is about 400 yen. We ordered a seafood pizza, and this place's pizza is the real thing, baked in a stone oven after you order. Being an island nation, all the seafood was delicious and satisfying. Though pizza doesn't feel Indonesian at all.
To the next day
Day 4 — Beautiful Meno Wall

Last night the power stayed on and we slept soundly. Our lodging is about 300 m in from the main street. Heading to the main street for breakfast, someone was selling bananas by the road. Lots of children around.

We found a diner where it was hard to tell whether it was open, and looking at the menu outside, the prices were reasonable, so we went in. It had a garden and didn't look very commercial, but the breakfast of bread, coffee and a fruit cocktail was just right. And the weather was perfect. A beautiful blue sky.

This morning was another pool dive. We practised all sorts of basic techniques: buoyancy control, what to do if your mask or regulator comes off, and so on. Of course our cameras couldn't get wet, but the instructor took photos with a camera in a waterproof case. I once went snorkelling in the sea, and remember it being very awkward, with water getting in. But breathing through a regulator was easier than expected, and I didn't swallow much seawater.
The waves were calm. In the afternoon, open-water training again. Our destination by boat: Meno Wall.

On the signal, into the sea. If you can't equalise properly your ears really hurt. Today Yamabe was off form; he couldn't clear his ears without straining hard. Ooi, on the other hand, seemed to have got the knack, and could now clear his ears without pinching his nose.

We gradually went deeper. The almost weightless feeling was pleasant. On land the heavy tank weighs down on your shoulders, but underwater you don't feel its weight at all. You forget you're carrying it.

On the seabed was a huge wall. This is Meno Wall. This wall, which seems to be made of coral reef, appeared to be home to countless fish. I don't know much about fish, so I had no idea what any of them were called, but I could tell that a great many kinds lived there. This photo was taken with an underwater camera borrowed from the instructor.
This is the familiar Nemo. It really was playing hide-and-seek in a sea anemone. They seem to like particular anemones with tube-like tentacles like this. It never tried to come out.
Fish so beautiful you can't stop looking. To think that fish like the ones I've seen in tropical-fish shops were swimming so leisurely in the wide ocean.
Found a pufferfish! Was it feeling poorly, or is it just that kind of fish? It stayed still on the seabed. Its blue eyes are distinctive.

We found something like a black haze on the seabed, and getting closer, we saw it was a gathering of small fish. Seen from a distance as they move, they look just like a big fish swimming. Maybe this is how they protect themselves from predators. Apparently they're called zebrafish.
A small fish came close. A transparent fish; you could see right down to its bones.
We met a moray eel too!! Its teeth were very sharp; put your hand out and it looked like it would bite. This one had blue eyes too.
After about 40 minutes underwater, we surfaced.
After a hugely satisfying dive, as we headed back to our lodging, people in a square were preparing something. It looked like a ring for martial arts.

When we came back to the square after changing, they were doing a martial art where fighters hit each other with shields and sticks. It seemed to be a festival day. In this sport, on the referee's signal the fighters close the distance and then just keep striking each other with sticks, but we couldn't work out how the winner was decided. When the fighting heated up, the bout seemed to end straight away. I think each bout lasted under a minute. What was interesting was how the matches were decided. It was like village against village, with a team in each corner, taunting each other with an air of "You come out next!" "I'll take you on!", and the matches got decided with a "Bring it on."

It was a little cloudy, but in the distance we could see Mt. Rinjani on the main island of Lombok. Apparently you can climb it on a guided three-night trek for a little over 10,000 yen, which really tempted me, but we had to give up because of time. It's Indonesia's third-highest peak, after Puncak Jaya in Papua and Mt. Kerinci in Sumatra, about the same height as Mt. Fuji.
Bought a bracelet while out walking. Haggling is a keyword everywhere in Indonesia. Even when you haggle, the other person rarely looks unhappy. If anything, they seem to enjoy it.
The sun was setting, so to a restaurant. Today we ordered an omelette and curry rice. The curry wasn't that spicy either; it was completely European-style.
To the next day
Day 5 — Shark Point & Coral Fun Garden

Already the morning of our fifth day since coming to Indonesia. I love this balcony. Even when it's humid, even when a squall is falling, if you just zone out here time slips by before you know it. It's hard to believe that in Japan I was buried in my thesis and part-time job. Today there were two open-water training dives, morning and afternoon. Training, but really it's like a free walk underwater while using what we'd learned from the videos and in the pool, so it's very enjoyable. In the morning we first enjoyed a dive at a spot called Shark Point, where sharks often appear. We took photos today too, but sadly they weren't on the CD-ROM we were given later. There weren't many small fish at Shark Point, and it felt a bit lonely. But it was quite deep, and we could go down to 20 m, beyond the Open Water limit. The water was a little cooler than near the surface, but even so we never felt cold at all.

At lunch we ordered fresh papaya and avocado juices. Being able to enjoy rich fresh juice for under 100 yen is a big attraction of this country, but the avocado juice was so thick that it was less like juice and more like protein cream. I can't say it tasted very good either. The papaya juice, on the other hand, had a tropical feel and tasted good. After this came the afternoon open-water training. The stage for our last open-water dive was Coral Fun Garden. Again we went beyond 20 m. Not only lots of tropical fish, but we also met a sea turtle and, though only one, a shark that swept past, and yet the photos that should have been taken weren't on the CD-ROM, just like the morning's, which was a real shame. If I ever go diving again, I definitely want to bring my own camera in a waterproof case.

After finishing all our open-water training, a walk along the main street. The horses that work hard on this island. Even when their owner leaves the cart on an errand, they wait obediently. Impressive.
To the next day
Day 6 — The final exam, and farewell to Trawangan

Pleasantly sunny again from the morning. At midday today we would take a written test on diving, and by getting a pass mark we could get our final certification (C-card). On the way from our lodging to the main street there is a primary school, and today again they were doing morning exercises.

Revising before the exam at a café bar on the beach. Apparently when you dive deep, nitrogen builds up in your body, and if you surface suddenly it forms bubbles inside you. This is called decompression sickness, and to prevent it you have to calculate your no-decompression limit from your depth. The card in my hand is the tool for that. The result...

We both got a pass mark and got our licences. A commemorative photo with our instructor and a man who happened to be there. Thank you so much. It was only four days, but the days we spent learning at this diving school became very memorable.

We would go back to the main island of Lombok at 4 p.m., so with time until then we decided to walk to the island's viewpoint, the top of a small hill almost in the middle of Gili Trawangan. Intense sunlight poured down from almost directly overhead. On the way there were cattle grazing.

From the hill we could see the neighbouring island of Gili Meno, Gili Air beyond it, and Mt. Rinjani on Lombok hidden in cloud. Thinking we were saying goodbye today to these islands ringed with coral, we were very sorry to leave.
It was nearly midday, so the sun beat down from almost directly overhead. So shadows formed almost only right at our feet.

After our walk we came back to the front of the dive shop. This is a map of the dive sites around the three Gili islands. We enjoyed diving at four of them: Bounty, Meno Wall, Shark Point and Coral Fun Garden. Looking at this, it's as if the three Gilis sit in the middle of a diving spot.
Goodbye, Gili Trawangan. And the people of Dream Divers.

That day we headed to a town called Senggigi on Lombok, where we stayed when we first came to the island. Raja's Bungalows, where we stayed then, was very comfortable but a little pricey (even so, about 750 yen each a night), so to cut our lodging costs a bit we chose New Pondok Sinta. The facilities were perfect, and above all it was big. And only 400 yen each a night, amazingly.
While Yamabe was checking in, Ooi found a monitor lizard behind the lodging! He hurriedly took a photo, but can you see where it is in this photo? Its back is captured near the middle of the photo.
Perhaps the owner was being thoughtful since it was two men staying. In the room was a portrait of a woman. Ooi is gazing at it, enchanted.

Dinner at a nearby warung (diner). We ordered pasta and nasi goreng with krupuk and a fried egg. After this we went to the front of the dive shop office in Senggigi. Why? Because when we arrived in Senggigi we had visited the instructor's home and been invited to a sate ayam (chicken skewer) party in the evening. But when we got there, nobody was around. Had we got the time wrong? We waited a while but nobody came, so we reluctantly went back to the lodging and went to bed. About a week since leaving Japan. The first stage of our trip, getting our diving licences, had ended safely. Tomorrow was finally the day we would meet KEN, who was coming alone from Japan, at last freed from his research. The second stage: a jungle expedition on Sumatra, an island bigger than all of Japan.
To the next day
Day 7 — A new companion, KEN

Our flight back to Jakarta left in the evening, so first we called at the instructor's home to apologise for not making it to the sate ayam party yesterday. This is the speargun the instructor uses to catch squid and so on when he dives. You pull the rubber band attached to it as hard as you can and hook it onto the fitting. Pull the trigger and the metal spear flies out with tremendous force.
Then we went out to Senggigi beach. The sea was blue and the waves calm. And again today, intense sunlight poured down.

Walking along the beach, a man selling spinning tops called us over. They were handmade tops, and thanks to a hole in the side, spin one hard and it makes a whistling sound. Ooi haggled and bought two.

We still had plenty of time, so to soothe our diving fatigue and look after our sunburnt skin we went to a massage place. An hour's full-body massage cost 750 yen. Astonishingly cheap. A little mishap happened here, so Ooi was staring out to sea in a daze.

Back to a warung for lunch. Here Ooi, who loves children, played with a little girl with the top. In the end he gave one of the tops to the girl. At first he only meant to lend it, but the girl seemed delighted, thinking it was a present. Good-natured Ooi didn't ask for it back and just watched her with a smile.

It was still quite early, but we took a taxi to the airport at Mataram. When we came here from Jakarta it was night, and we got into a taxi straight away, so we hadn't really seen the airport, but it was a very compact airport, and with the city around it, it had a very relaxed atmosphere.

We had a lot of time to spare, so we explored the area. There wasn't much to see, but a part-timer in front of a Yamaha motorbike shop called out to us. He said he was a student at the University of Mataram, in the engineering faculty. He spoke fluent English and looked clearly bright. Indonesians usually speak English as if reading it in Indonesian. For example, they pronounce "Air" as "ai-ru".

We went through security to the departure lounge. In Indonesia, airport tax and so on isn't included in the ticket. So you have to pay it directly at a counter at the airport. It's fairly expensive; at Mataram airport we had to pay about 350 yen.
This is the ticket. The blue paper at the top right is proof of paying the airport tax. All in all, very flimsy scraps of paper.

Unlike Batavia Air on the way out, Lion Air made the announcement exactly on time. We queued, showed our tickets and walked out of the building straight onto the runway. A world away from Centrair or Jakarta. Passengers walk straight to the plane and board by the stairs.

Aboard the plane. The air conditioning worked well, and the plane looked fairly new. Cheaper than Batavia, and Lion Air isn't bad at all (lol). And as on Batavia, the flight attendants all had great figures and were beautiful. Lion Air's in particular wore uniforms like a cheongsam with an Indonesian-style pattern, with daring slits up to the thigh showing bare legs; quite sexy. After all, on Batavia Air's website, in the recruitment section for flight attendants, the first requirement is "nice looks", then "nice figure", and only third "able to speak English". And there's an age requirement of 20 to 30. In Japan such blatant discrimination would probably be a scandal. Maybe Indonesian businessmen who like women choose their airline by the flight attendants.
Arrived in Jakarta. Unlike when we came from Japan, it didn't feel very humid. We seemed to have got quite used to the heat.
While waiting for our checked bags, I went to the toilet and there was a tank in front of the urinals with goldfish swimming in it.

To wait for KEN's arrival, we moved to the international terminal. First we phoned the rental car company man and met up. We told him our friend's flight and he agreed to wait until then. To kill time, A&W again.
Like the locals, we prepared something like this and waited for KEN to arrive.
KEN arrived. Like us, he came via Hong Kong on Cathay Pacific. He said he'd been swamped with research until yesterday.

The rental company man drove us to a hotel, which was nice, but unfortunately many places were already full, and only at about the fifth did we finally find one with a room. A bit pricey, about 2,600 yen for the three of us. But it had a hot shower and the room was faultless. It even had a TV. Tomorrow we would land on Sumatra.
To the next day
Day 8 — Across the Sunda Strait to Sumatra

Going out onto the street in front of the hotel before breakfast, there was a huge morning traffic jam. Unlike Japan, there were more motorbikes than cars, weaving between the cars, each trying to get ahead. An overwhelming sight.
This hotel included breakfast. We expected something simple like toast, but it was nasi goreng with krupuk.

There was still time before the rental company man came, so we explored the town a little. There was a lot of rubbish around, and in places a foul smell. There was a river too, but it was very dirty, with lots of rubbish floating in it.

When we got back to the hotel the rental company man had arrived, and we paid the final contract money of a little over 60,000 yen. Our journey to Sumatra with a Daihatsu Xenia was supposed to begin. As we got into the car in high spirits to set off, a scruffily dressed man was making a fuss outside. When we talked, with the company man, he said he was the driver. That wasn't what we agreed. Even when we said we didn't need a driver, they wouldn't give way. We did not want to spend about two weeks together with him. And how were we supposed to pay for his food and lodging? As we kept talking, we were told we wouldn't have to pay him another penny, so take him along. And that we should go wherever we wanted without holding back and enjoy our trip as we liked. We would later deeply regret compromising here, but we reluctantly agreed to travel with the driver.

After leaving the hotel, the car headed off in a direction we didn't understand. Worried, we asked, and he said he was stopping at his home to pick up a change of clothes and so on. We wish he'd told us first, but when we tried to explain the route ahead, the driver didn't understand English. The only English he understood was OK and money. But picking up clothes: where had he come from this morning? If he'd come from home, he could have brought everything then.
We got on the expressway and headed for Merak at the western tip of Java. The driver drove roughly, and there were many hair-raising moments on the way.
Out of Jakarta, farmland spread out.
Merak is also the end of the expressway. We had driven 100 km, but the toll was only a little over 300 yen, very cheap.
When we reached the port we thought we'd have lunch, so using our point-and-speak phrasebook we asked the driver if there was a good place, and he stopped at a nearby restaurant.

It was a Padang restaurant. Padang food comes from the town of Padang on Sumatra, and when you sit down, lots of dishes are brought out on small plates. Customers eat only the dishes they like and pay after the meal for what they ate. So rather than nibbling a little from many plates, it's better to finish any plate you start. After the meal, looking at the bill, it came to over 2,000 yen, about three times our usual food budget. Far too expensive... While we stood dumbfounded, the driver said "money money" and pulled notes out of KEN's wallet. More than the amount on the bill, too. What is he doing, we thought; we stopped him and handed the money to the staff ourselves, and the amount was enough. The driver didn't pay for what he had eaten. I think our trust in the driver collapsed from this moment.
We loaded the car onto the ferry and set sail. Sumatra was already visible in the distance.
On the top deck of the ship there was something like a live concert. Incredibly loud.

The man sitting next to us at the concert was a member of the crew, and when he learned we were Japanese he invited us into the wheelhouse. Many of the instruments in the wheelhouse were labelled in Japanese. The ship was built more than 40 years ago, and must once have been in service in Japan.
Sumatra was close. Small islands dotted the area near Bakauheni port, and checking the shore with binoculars, it was a mangrove coast.

After docking we were kept waiting over an hour until the ferry's gate opened. There were lots of buses and big trucks around with their engines running, so the smell of exhaust was terrible. Meanwhile we tried to communicate with the driver using the phrasebook. We meant to give him directions for the road ahead, but he didn't seem very interested in listening.

Landed on Sumatra!! The first thing to greet us was jungle as far as the eye could see. It was amazing that this land, next to Java with its more than 100 million people, was still so untamed. The main road is one lane each way and the paving isn't great. Of course there are no expressways. We landed in the evening, so we couldn't drive far; we had planned to stay in Bandar Lampung but ended up staying in a town called Bintuhan, a little before it. The losmen we found looked like a ruin from outside, and when they showed us the room there were cobwebs and a horribly dirty bathroom-cum-toilet; one surprise after another. And the surprises kept coming. Despite all the talk of no extra charges, just as we chose a room and were about to go in, the driver started shouting, "Where's my room?" We were dumbfounded and insisted that we had an agreement, but the driver wouldn't back down. Going back and forth with the phrasebook again, he said he didn't want to continue the trip. We didn't want to continue with the driver either. We never wanted to bring him in the first place. Even when we said we would drive the car ourselves and he should go back to Jakarta with this money, he wouldn't agree. The lodging's owner joined in and there was a long discussion, and in the end, because we wanted to keep travelling, we gave way and finally agreed to pay him 90,000 rupiah a day. The driver only listens when you pile on money. By giving way here, we set off the worst kind of downward spiral.

Exhausted after the discussion with the driver, we didn't have much appetite, but we went to a nearby food stall and ordered nasi goreng with fried chicken. The stall owner was an old man with hardly any teeth left, a little eerie-looking, but very friendly and good at English. Thanks to him we even learned some Indonesian, like how to count. He was kind and explained the bill clearly too. It felt as though our hearts, wounded by the fierce battle with the driver, were healing.
To the next day
Day 9 — Bukit Barisan Selatan National Park
This is the losmen (cheap lodging) we stayed in. The three of us shared one bed, but we were tired, so we slept without any problem.
We went for a morning walk. We could see all the way round the bay. Amazingly, people live right at the water's edge.
Breakfast at the stall where we had dinner last night. He made us instant noodles. We bought some kue (snacks) too, but the meal cost under 100 yen each, astonishingly cheap.

The driver's outrages didn't stop. He even charged us for an oil change. He had even changed the oil filter, though we hadn't yet driven 1,000 km. And he was driving quite far off the road we had specified. In short, he'd got lost. We talked it over with the oil-change shop staff too, but neither the driver nor the staff seemed to know how to read a map.

In the end, by a big detour, we managed to reach our goal, the World Heritage site of Bukit Barisan Selatan National Park. The decisive difference from Japanese forests is the density of the plants. A truly dense jungle. I felt its powerful life force.
This red soil is probably laterite.

Refuelling. In Indonesia we only saw Pertamina petrol stations. Petrol and diesel were the same price, about 45 yen a litre. Cheap!! As you'd expect of an oil-producing country. On Sumatra too, high-quality crude oil is produced in quantity at places like the Minas oil field near Pekanbaru.

The road through the national park stayed rough, and our average speed fell to about 20 km/h. It was full of potholes, and there was no way to speed up with any confidence. The jungle pressed in close, so we could hardly see ahead. We kept driving and finally came out on the south-west coast. The waves of the Indian Ocean were strong, and for some reason the sea was a cloudy yellowish colour. But there was no bad smell, and no rubbish scattered on the beach. The sunset was beautiful.

The state of the roads on Sumatra, and inside the national park at that, completely exceeded our expectations. We had really wanted to get to Bengkulu today, but it was impossible. A miscalculation, and our mistake. We had dinner before reaching our lodging. A simple buffet-style restaurant, with countless geckos crawling on the walls. In the end we reached a hotel in a town called Pajang at about 10 p.m. It was a cheap hotel, but a little pricier than a losmen, so we gave the driver the amount over his daily allowance. I still can't forget the driver's fearless grin when we handed him the money.
To the next day
Day 10 — The driver runs amok

Tiring days continued, but sleep did restore our strength. Spending our days with the driver, though, was mentally hard. Ooi in particular had been in the passenger seat the whole time, so his stress was far beyond mine. What surprise would await us today? In the morning we ate curry at a buffet-style diner right near the hotel.
Maybe today was some special day. Events like this were being held in various places. At first I thought it was a wedding, but apparently not. Music was blaring from huge speakers.
To Bengkulu the road follows the coast the whole way. Compared with yesterday, relatively good straight road continued, but here and there were unpaved places that looked badly gouged out.
A short break where we could see a beautiful beach. Again the sea was cloudy and yellow. Pleasant sunshine.
Coconuts, now a very familiar sight in Indonesia. These had fallen on the shore.

We reached Bengkulu around midday, but here too there was a problem. The driver threw a tantrum, saying he was tired. At one point he was making childish demands that he didn't want to leave Bengkulu, but that was no good. If we didn't leave Bengkulu, we would fall a whole day behind schedule. After more exhausting negotiations, we agreed he would take us to a town called Kepahiang, a little under 100 km north-east of Bengkulu. But after this the driver ran amok, driving off in completely the wrong direction. We showed him the map, saying we are here, you've taken the wrong road, go back, but he wouldn't listen at all. When he felt unsure of the road, he would stop the car and ask people nearby. Many Indonesians, out of kindness, can't bring themselves to say "I don't know". It may be prejudiced, of course, but most people on Sumatra didn't seem to know how to read a map. He valued what such people said over the map, so we couldn't go the way we wanted. The car moved further away from our final destination, Bukittinggi on the equator, and if anything closer to Java. The sun set, and the car kept driving along remote country roads. We passed many similar settlements, and when we told him to go left at an important junction, he said no. Was he planning to go straight back to Jakarta? Fed up, we demanded quite forcefully that he go left, but he threatened us with gestures like slitting a throat, saying bandits would come out. To the end he didn't follow our instructions and went right. We were completely appalled. Again today we reached our lodging in Pagar Alam very late. We had no time to find a cheap place and ended up at a hotel, but the whole responsibility for today's mistake was his, so we didn't give him any extra money.

A heavy atmosphere hung over the hotel room. We never thought we would be so unable to travel the way we wanted. This made renting a car pointless. It felt like riding in a runaway car with no idea where it was going. In Indonesia transport is cheap; even flying costs less than travelling by train in Japan. The reason we deliberately rented a car was that we wanted to see places you can't experience travelling by plane.

We decided to part ways with the driver. The idea had come up while we were still in the car, but it was to get him to take us at least as far as Bukittinggi on the equator and then give him the slip. But at this pace it seemed certain we could never reach Bukittinggi in the time we had. On top of that, we had reached our limit of being in the same space as a driver who would never try to understand us. We decided to get up a little early tomorrow morning and leave this town, leaving the driver and the car behind. From tomorrow we would lose our wheels, but the thought of travelling freely on our own made us excited.
To the next day
Day 11 — Parting with the driver, and taken to the police station

A light rain was falling, but it felt like the most refreshing morning yet. At last we would be free of that wretched, reckless driver. We could have left without a word, but as a courtesy we left a note. It said that the driver and the rental company had completely broken their agreement with us, so he should go back to Jakarta with the car. We didn't think there would be buses from Pagar Alam to Bukittinggi, so we thought we would head for the town of Lahat, on the road running the length of Sumatra, which was probably on the route of long-distance buses from Jakarta to Bukittinggi. First we had to get to the bus terminal.
A passing vehicle honked to signal to us. It seemed to be a shared taxi (bemo). It agreed to take us to the bus terminal for Lahat.

At first the driver seemed confident he'd take us to the bus terminal, but partway it began to feel doubtful whether he knew or not, so we had him go back to a place where several buses were parked and got out of the bemo. When we asked at the counter, they said there was a bus to Lahat! We couldn't hide our excitement: now we could completely escape the driver.

From the window of the bus to Lahat we again saw jungle as far as the eye could see. The rain stopped and the sun peeked out. It seemed to show that our journey ahead would go well, but in fact it didn't. We reached Lahat all right, but the bus wandered around the town for a while and then dropped us in front of the police station. We didn't want to get off, but the bus crew told us to, so we had no choice. The police asked to see our passports and told us to wait at the station for a while. At first I thought it was something like a checkpoint before entering the town, but Ooi guessed the driver had reported us. At first I dismissed it, but Ooi's guess turned out exactly right. The police officers were all friendly, and the good part was being treated to lunch for free: a hot meal even tastier than what we'd been eating. After about an hour's wait, the driver arrived in that car with a police officer from Pagar Alam. Now there was nothing for it but to stop running and hiding and honestly explain the ordeal we'd been through. Fortunately English got through to the police to some extent, and one officer let us talk on the phone with someone who understood some Japanese. We stressed that we had been deceived, and our case that we didn't want to travel with the driver any more was accepted. The driver looked very bitter. He then demanded that we pay his travel and food costs home, but no way. If we had been willing to do that, we would obviously have paid in advance before parting. The officers said, don't worry now, we'll take you to a bus stop for Bukittinggi. At that point we trusted them. We thought it was very kind. But after going round various towns, they said there was no suitable bus in this town and started heading for a town in the opposite direction from Bukittinggi. The sun was about to set. Before we reached that town, they stopped a bus coming the other way and told us to get on it. But the amount they told us to pay was about twice what it would cost to fly from Jakarta to Padang, the city near Bukittinggi. Even for a VIP-class bus, that was outrageous. The officers kept straight faces, but they surely had that much sense of money. The bus driver may have been overcharging, but there was no doubt the officers would get a cut too. If we paid that much, there was a big chance our trip would run aground partway. We stressed to the officers that we had no money, declined their offer and begged them to turn back. The officers looked exasperated and disappointed. They must have expected to get a lot of money. We were glad of their kindness, but it's a problem to be expected to pay money when we were travelling on a budget. We thought if we went back to Lahat, where the police station was, the officers would again inflict unwanted favours on us, so we asked to be dropped in a town called Muara Enim on the way. The journey from where we turned back to Muara Enim felt really long. I wanted them to let us go soon. We had no idea where to stay in Muara Enim, but we were dropped somewhere fairly busy. We didn't want anything more to do with the officers, but sure enough, they told us to pay their travel costs back. Exactly as predicted. I became suspicious of everything, and, shamefully, at that moment I even had the biased thought that I couldn't trust Indonesians at all. It's true they looked after us, but nothing they did for us was actually helpful. How much better it would have been if they'd just released us at the police station in Lahat.

Once they asked for money, we said we had none, walked briskly away from them and wandered the streets with no destination. Then, luckily, we found a sign saying "Losmen this way". This place was amazingly cheap, a little over 200 yen each. It was simply built, but nothing like as awful as the losmen in Bintuhan. Today may have been the most tiring day yet. We didn't feel we had done anything wrong, so strangely we didn't panic, but the stress of being held again just when we thought we were free of the driver was huge, and keeping up a friendly face for money-hungry police officers was hard. But now, from tomorrow, we should really be able to enjoy travelling, just the three of us.
To the next day
Day 12 — By long-distance bus to Bukittinggi!

We woke at about 6:30 a.m. to the sound of the lodging staff knocking on the door. This place even included breakfast (a set of instant mie goreng and coffee). Last night they had brought an extra bed too; full marks for service at that price. We ate breakfast looking at the courtyard, and after checking out we had to quickly find a bus to Bukittinggi. For three days we had been moving, yet we hadn't got any closer to Bukittinggi at all. Bukittinggi is a scenic tourist spot about 50 km south of the equator, and joining a jungle trekking tour run nearby was our main goal in travelling on Sumatra.

We went to something like a bus terminal and asked whether there was a bus to Bukittinggi, and there was. It was a little expensive, so we haggled down to what seemed a fair price. But the ticket counter felt shady, so we didn't pay straight away; we said we'd pay once they showed us the bus, and they agreed. After waiting at the terminal for a while, a small van came and told us to get in. It seemed we wouldn't board the bus here but at a bus depot a little way off. During the hour and a half we waited, we enjoyed chatting with the man from the ticket counter who came with us. He loved singing, and played a Hideaki Tokunaga song on his phone and sang for us. The bus had working air conditioning but was clearly not VIP class: an ultra-long-distance bus from Palembang to Medan. Now and then it stopped and vendors got on to sell food. Music was also blaring inside the bus.
We passed through town after town. Reading made me carsick, so we passed the time eating snacks and so on.
Hard to see, but those are chickens crammed into wooden crates. No doubt at all they're destined to be eaten.

Late at night, while I was sleeping, KEN suddenly woke me just before midnight and said we were getting off. We were supposed to reach Bukittinggi the next morning, and looking around, it didn't look like Bukittinggi. Half asleep, I was very confused. It was a cheap bus, so were we being abandoned here? But when we asked a nearby person who got off with us, it turned out we were changing buses here. After waiting by the road for a while, a bus did come. We got on and headed for Bukittinggi again.
To the next day
Day 13 — An idyll on the equator

After a 20-hour journey, we arrived in Bukittinggi from Muara Enim. We arrived before 6 a.m. when it was still dim, so many shops around the bus terminal hadn't opened yet, but even here taxi drivers kept calling out to us. First, after being cramped in a narrow bus for so long, we were hungry. So we decided to have breakfast at Simpang Raya, a reasonably priced Padang restaurant listed in our guidebook. I'm not sure whether it's because this is the home of Padang food or just because it was early, but the food and rice here weren't cold like what we'd eaten so far; they were steaming hot.
There were rounded mountains around the highland city of Bukittinggi. The photo below is probably the famous Mt. Singgalang.

We meant to go from the bus terminal to the town centre, but we completely misread the map and at first couldn't get there. There was a magnificent mosque, unlike anything we'd seen in the towns of Sumatra so far.
Is this a durian?
In a square where locals gather we found a huge climbing wall. Around here we finally managed to work out where we were.

This building with its distinctive roof is a traditional Minangkabau house, its shape modelled on buffalo horns. The Minangkabau are one of the world's rare matrilineal peoples, and apparently ownership of houses and so on all rests with women.

The town centre was bursting with life. It's a hilly town, with many stairways. Lots of souvenir shops lined the streets, somehow reminiscent of Kyoto, and the atmosphere was completely different from the towns so far. And the highland city of Bukittinggi is at about 900 m. So even when the sun is high, the temperature and humidity don't rise that much, and it's very comfortable.

Bukittinggi used to be a fortress town. The fort from that time is called Fort de Kock, and it's now a museum popular with tourists. This is a footbridge, but it's in a spot you can't cross without entering the museum. In the end we never went into the museum.

First we decided to look for lodging. Merdeka Homestay, listed in our guidebook, was only 300 yen each, yet the room was clean and spacious, with a hot shower (it turns cold after about 5 minutes)! As you'd expect of a tourist spot! As you'd expect of Bukittinggi!
After a rest at the lodging, we went back into town for lunch. Many of the houses were fairly nice, and a cat was napping on a windowsill. The cats in this town have good coats and aren't dirty.

Everything so far had been spicy, so all of us except KEN had kept having stomach trouble. So we said let's eat Chinese food, and went into a place called Monalisa. The interior was plain, with a famous oil painting of the Mona Lisa hanging on the back wall. Disappointingly, even though it was a Chinese restaurant, "chinjao rosu" didn't get through at all. The menu didn't list Chinese dish names either; it was written in Indonesian, so for some dishes we had to look things up in the phrasebook to know what was what. The food was all delicious and satisfying, but we were shocked when we saw the bill after the meal! Over 200,000 rupiah, nearly three nights' lodging. That's expensive... We planned to stay three nights in Bukittinggi, but we'd never come here again. And I thought that at places without prices on the menu, we must check properly beforehand.

After lunch we went to a travel agency and bought tomorrow's jungle trek, a rental motorbike for the day after, and plane tickets to return to Jakarta the day after that. We successfully haggled down the jungle trek and the bike rental, to about 2,000 yen and 600 yen respectively.

We got caught in the rain on the way back to the lodging. Heavy rain continued after that, and when it stopped in the evening we set off into town for dinner, and there were five or six monkeys on the roofs of houses and so on.

Dinner was at Texas Chicken, a fast-food place inside a department store in the centre of town. This set was about 400 yen. Not that cheap compared with other restaurants. It even had a proper mascot character.

After dinner we went to the square in front of the clock tower, the town's symbol, near the department store. There were street stalls in the square, and a man was playing with something like a glowing bamboo-copter. He wasn't playing seriously; he was showing it to children to sell it.
To the next day
Day 14 — The jungle trek of our dreams

Our main reason for coming to Indonesia was jungle trekking in Indonesia. Today was the day that goal would be fulfilled. It was really meant to be a road trip: on the way out we would mainly drive the west side of Sumatra along the Barisan Mountains, and on the way back the great plains spreading across eastern Sumatra, through Pekanbaru, Jambi, Palembang and so on, but after a series of troubles that became impossible, so we would fly back to Jakarta from Padang. When troubles struck and we had to change our plans, our top priority was here: jungle trekking in Bukittinggi.
A cicada and a snail we found when we went out for breakfast. Both a little different from the Japanese ones.
In the morning the guide came to pick us up from our lodging.

The trek begins! The stage for the trek was the Ngarai Sianok canyon near Bukittinggi, known as the Grand Canyon of Sumatra. There was no signpost at the start; we descended to the bottom of the canyon following a trodden path. The guide spoke fluent English, and was kind enough to explain all about the jungle, plants and so on, as we walked.
As we threaded our way down to the bottom of the valley between the dense trees, a muddy brown river came into view. It seemed to be flowing very fast.
The rainforest is made up mainly of tall broadleaf trees, but small plants also live near the ground, where only a little sunlight reaches.
Reaching the bottom of the valley, the usual path had unfortunately been washed away by the river.
So we crossed the river in a chain, holding on to each other. I thought it would be a gentler trek, so doing something like this right at the start was a huge surprise!

Right after crossing the river, we were greeted by the world's largest flower, the rafflesia. The guide had told us beforehand that it had withered three days ago, so we were surprised. Sure enough, next to this flower were the blackened remains. More rotten than withered.
The inside of the flower is spiky and a little grotesque.
Look how big it is compared with a person!!
We followed a path with no signposts, and climbed up a stream we thought we would just cross. A truly wild trek. And leeches appeared, like the ones you often meet in Japanese mountain streams!
A short break beside the stream. There was a butterfly that looked like it could live in Japan too.

From the bottom of the canyon, the climb began. During a short break on the slope, the guide said this tree is cinnamon, took out a knife and started cutting off the bark. He gave us a piece of bark, and when we smelled it, it really was cinnamon itself. I didn't know cinnamon came from trees like this.
At the top of the slope, banana plantations spread out. We were already in the area where people live.
The weather was fine, very peaceful.
We also met a pill bug as big as a thumb.
Hanging from the trunk are papayas.
Cacao pods sprout straight out of the trunk too.
This green fruit is avocado.
A short break at a kiosk. In the field in front of us, water buffalo were bathing.
Perhaps foreigners were a rarity; children followed us, laughing. The girls must have been shy: when I pointed the camera at them they squealed and ran away.
Peeled cacao beans were drying in front of a house.
Red and green berries. These are coffee beans. When we peeled one, it really was shaped like a coffee bean. They're green before roasting.
Women carried loads on their heads, deftly keeping their balance.
This is the Ngarai Sianok canyon, along whose bottom we had walked.
With Mt. Singgalang in the distance, we walked along a paved road.
Eventually the road turned to dirt again, and as we went down the zigzag slope, a water buffalo came up from below, being whipped on the rump.
Back down at the bottom of the canyon, the path became a trail only people could use. In reality, though, several motorbikes came and went.
Lunchtime on a riverbank with a striking, oddly shaped rock in view. This nasi campur wrapped in a banana leaf was handmade by the guide's wife.
Mimosa (sensitive plant) on the riverbank.
A warty toad on the riverbank.
Goats on the riverbank.

Rice paddies spreading through the canyon. Apparently some areas of Sumatra grow three crops a year. Unlike Japan, it was quite normal to see one paddy just planted and another already being harvested.
Leaving the canyon, we walked through the town of Koto Gadang, famous for silverwork.
We tried to cross the canyon again to get back, but the path had collapsed and was impassable. We reluctantly caught a shared taxi back.

Walking from morning to evening, we were a little tired. For dinner we went to a slightly stylish restaurant. Nice for being reasonable despite how it looked: a steak set was about 300 yen. With trendy juices with little bits in them and a free jelly bar as a starter, it was a place that would be popular even in Japan.
To the next day
Day 15 — We stand on the equator

When we lost the rental car I had nearly given up on reaching the equator, but then the idea came up: why not rent motorbikes from Bukittinggi and go? However, Indonesia currently doesn't issue licences for tourists, and international licences can't be used, so it would be driving without a licence. But we had heard that even if we were caught by the police, a bribe of about 200 yen would get us let off, so we judged it would be fine.
We got breakfast at a bakery.
At the bakery, as well as bread, we bought a yokan-like sweet that seemed to be made from coconut milk.

The clouds hadn't looked good since we left the lodging in the morning, and just as we went to rent the bikes it started to rain. We killed time at a café restaurant for a while, and when the rain eased to a drizzle we headed for the equator, about 70 km north-east of Bukittinggi. The bikes we rented were the ordinary kind we'd seen in every Indonesian city, all made in Japan. Indonesia is a motorbike society, and almost all the bikes are Japanese. But the models differ from Japan's: a Super Cub chassis with scooter bodywork. I wondered why they don't give Japanese Cubs a design like this. The transmission, like the Cub, is a clutchless rotary manual. 125 cc, equivalent to a Japanese class-2 moped (pink plate).
The tank wasn't full, so first we refuelled. 45 yen a litre is very welcome. Like the Cub, the fuel tank is under the seat.
We rode on north-east along a winding road through dense jungle.
Terraced rice fields, rarely seen in Japan since mechanisation. Here ox carts were still hard at work.

There was little traffic and the riding was pleasant, but just 5 km south of the equator was the police checkpoint we had been worried about... We had 50,000 rupiah tucked in a pocket, but the officer was very friendly ☆ He asked where we were from, and when we said Japan, he even shook hands and said welcome. Yamabe showed the international licence he had got just in case, and Nakakura his Japanese licence, but Ooi hadn't brought anything like a licence. But the officer just showed us a local licence, saying really in Indonesia you need one of these, and told us to go on through without any reprimand.

A few minutes' ride from the checkpoint, we finally arrived right on the equator, where there's a gate. As we got off the bikes and soaked it in, a man came over showing off T-shirts. They were printed T-shirts with an equator motif you could only buy here, so all three of us bought different colours and took a commemorative photo.
It was still before noon, and waiting for the sun to reach its zenith would be hot and boring, so we rode a little further north-east and did some sightseeing in the town of Bonjol.

Then at noon, we came back to the equator. There was something like a memorial park nearby, with the equator marked by a white line in the grounds. We straddled it for a commemorative photo. As you can see, our shadows are only directly beneath us. It had been a long road to get here...

After the equator, our next goal was Lake Maninjau, about 50 km west of Bukittinggi. From the equator we had to go back to Bukittinggi first. We had lunch at a diner a little south of the equator. There was no air conditioning, but once in the shade it was surprisingly comfortable. In the sun, the glare off the ground was fierce too, a scorching heat.

On the way back to Bukittinggi after lunch, trouble: Ooi's bike ran out of petrol. There were no petrol stations nearby; as I remembered it, we'd have to go about 10 km to find one. Yamabe and KEN went to the petrol station and asked if there was anything to put petrol in, and they filled an empty plastic bottle that had been thrown in the bin. Something that would never be allowed in Japan.
Refuelled and back in action!
Riding on along a winding road from Bukittinggi, we reached a point looking down on a beautiful lake reflecting the sun. This is Lake Maninjau.
From that point down to the shore of Lake Maninjau, the road descends through 44 hairpins. Each corner had a sign showing its number, which was fun. And many monkeys appeared along this road.
We reached the lakeshore. If the water had been clean we were thinking of swimming, but there were dead fish floating, and it didn't make us feel like swimming.
Beautiful Lake Maninjau and the rainforest.
Climbing back up the 44 hairpins, the sky had turned a little red, if not quite a sunset.
As expected, monkeys appeared everywhere.
After returning the bikes at the café restaurant where we started, dinner. This feast was about 300 yen each. Bukittinggi being a tourist town, the restaurants were of a high standard.
To the next day
Day 16 — The old Japanese army tunnels
Today was the day we left Bukittinggi for Padang, where the airport is. Fort de Kock looked good, but our time was limited, so first we went to the old Japanese army air-raid tunnels.
Flamboyant costumes found in a department store. Traditional Minangkabau costumes, perhaps?
Before going to the tunnels we enjoyed shopping in the market. These are snacks piled up in huge quantities.
The market had a distinctive smell, probably given off by dried fish like these.
At the market we bought the classic bananas and an unusual fruit called salak.
Among the bananas we just bought were two joined together.
Peeled, the salak looked like garlic, but the smell wasn't strong, and it had an indescribable taste. A firm texture, and not very sweet.
Japanese manga were on sale all over the market too.

Mie bakso (noodles with meatballs), which I'd long wanted to try after seeing it in our food guidebook. It lived up to its reputation: not spicy, with the flavour of the meatballs coming through nicely. Very tasty!
At a stall, Ooi bought the durian dessert he'd been longing for. It looks a bit grotesque, but he was eating it saying "delicious, delicious". Taste is personal, though.
An assortment of sate ayam (chicken skewers) KEN bought at the next stall.

Entry to the old Japanese army tunnels was about 30 yen, and the area around the entrance was a park with a view over the Ngarai Sianok canyon. It was amazing how the edge of town suddenly turned into jungle.
This is the entrance. It runs deep down at an angle. Headlamps on, time to explore!
Inside, the passages formed a grid, and there even seemed to be toilets. If they'd wanted, they could probably have housed several thousand people.

Exploring inside, we found several things like emergency exits, but almost all had iron bars so you couldn't get out. One had an extremely small opening and no bars, so we went out and found ourselves halfway up a cliff leading down to the jungle. Right outside we also saw a big lizard, but it ran away at once, so we couldn't get a photo.

After exploring the tunnels, we caught a bus to Padang from the bus terminal. We thought we could just buy tickets at the counter, but lots of men called out to us, and we boarded after a lot of haggling.

On the way to Padang, the most powerful squall yet. On top of that, the bus didn't go into central Padang; we were dropped on the edge of town. Fortunately by then the rain had weakened a lot. Huge numbers of shared buses were running in Padang, all flashy-looking, some with horns that made strange sounds. We got one of these to take us to a lodging. We tried two places listed in our guidebook, but both cost about twice the listed price, so we gave up.

From the second place we searched for lodging on foot. It wasn't very cheap, but it was the cheapest of the ones we visited, so we settled on it and had dinner at KFC. Fried chicken was about 100 yen a piece, less than half the price in Japan! The taste was spicier than in Japan.
Back at the lodging we went straight to bed. Travelling for the first time in a while, and overwhelmed by the bustle of Padang, we were tired.
To the next day
Day 17 — Crazy City "Padang"
We meant to stay two nights in Padang, but there apparently aren't many sights. Today the plan was first to change money for KEN, who was nearly out of cash, and then swim at the beach.

After breakfast we walked to the city centre looking for a bank. The atmosphere was completely different from clean Bukittinggi. The pavements were rough, with conspicuous holes you could fall into the gutter through.

The Matahari department store in the city centre had collapsed; lots of stalls were set up around it, but there was no sign of business. We later learned it was from the earthquake last September. There should have been lots of banks around the department store, but there weren't that many. And maybe because it was Saturday, they weren't open...
Near the department store there was a market, where cute, colourful chicks were for sale, cheeping away. Poor chicks, dyed just to make them stand out.

The meat and fish section of this market was frighteningly unhygienic. On tables that we doubted were ever washed, they hacked huge chunks of meat and sold them, untroubled by the countless flies swarming over them. A foul smell filled the air, and the ground had pitch-black puddles like sludge.
Wilting in the hellish heat, we went back to the lodging for a short rest.
We went out looking for a bank again, but nothing seemed to be open, so we gave up on changing money.
While we were having lunch at a bakery, a student from the Padang Japanese Language Institute talked to us in broken Japanese.
The bakery was like a convenience store, selling lots of snacks too. Japanese labels stood out everywhere.
We went out to the beach in Padang, but it smelled a little.
On top of that, with something like this lying at the water's edge, you lose all desire to swim.

After sunbathing on the shore, we walked along the coast toward the old town. The river water was polluted, and thinking that this water flows into the sea, I felt we were right not to swim. The old town had declined completely, with many half-collapsed buildings. And where had the Chinatown that should have been there gone?

The city centre was jammed with astonishing numbers of shared taxis. The honking was deafening. On top of that, they play music at full volume inside. The drivers are usually young guys. Why have this town's shared taxis ended up like this? By the way, in this town they're called angkot rather than bemo. I couldn't really bring myself to like them.
The beach at dusk.
There were some inappropriate parts in what was written on this page, so I would like to add a note.

On 30 September 2009, an earthquake struck off Padang, and more than 1,000 people lost their lives in the city of Padang too. The half-collapsed buildings we saw, and the market lining the streets near the department store, all told of the scars left by the earthquake. In the title I described all this as Crazy. I don't think that was wrong, but I must say here that it was something woven by the energy of people working toward recovery.

The children we met in a city that had begun moving toward recovery never stopped smiling. The future of this country, rich in both resources and people, is bright, and for us Japanese these Japan-friendly people may one day be partners with whom we should build even stronger ties than with China.
To the next day
Day 18 — Farewell to Sumatra
Today was the day we flew Batavia Air back to good old Java, to Jakarta.
Yamabe was down with a stomach ache from the morning. KEN and Ooi had breakfast at yesterday's bakery.
A children's drawing contest being held in the square in front of a nearby bank.
Splitting up: Yamabe
Yamabe, who wasn't feeling well since midday, went separately from the other two.
First, to fill my stomach, to Texas Chicken, which they also had in the department store in Bukittinggi.

I wasn't feeling well, so I meant to stay in the restaurant the whole time, but that was boring, so I went to a museum right near Texas Chicken, about 15 yen to enter, introducing Minangkabau history and so on.
Stuffed animals, including the smallest tiger, the Sumatran tiger.

About 15 minutes after I went into the museum, a group of girls surrounded me and asked if I had some time. Our meeting point was the bus stop for the airport, and I still had just under two hours, so I said OK, and the girls squealed with delight; one of the group clung to me, pressing tight against my shoulder, and like that they took me to a nearby something-or-other school. Somewhere along the way my stomach ache had completely gone. These girls were local high-school students, about 16 years old. The place we were going seemed to be something like the international school they attend.

I was warmly welcomed at the school too, talked with the teachers about Japan and Indonesia, and a teacher gave me a lift to the bus stop on his motorbike. It turned into a fulfilling time I could never have imagined that morning while battling my stomach ache.
Splitting up: Ooi & KEN
The two headed for Siti Nurbaya Park, a little way from the lodging.
But all they saw were derelict buildings, a goat and a drowned goat, and thanks to locals giving unwanted directions they couldn't even reach the park, and ended up back at the bus stop.

After waiting about an hour at the bus stop, a DAMRI bus, which had also helped us in Jakarta, finally came. The airport building was modelled on a traditional Minangkabau house and had a nice atmosphere.

After checking in and waiting in the lounge for a while, the announcement came right on time. Well done, Batavia Air! Padang airport is also a simple building with nothing around it. Unlike Mataram airport, there was a proper walkway to the plane.
The sunset seen from the plane on the way to Jakarta.
There was no in-flight meal, but they gave us a sweet bun and water.
Arrived in Jakarta for the first time in about ten days!
We had booked a cheap lodging by phone, so we had plenty of time. Dinner was our third A&W at the airport.
To the next day
Day 19 — Shopping in Jakarta

Tomorrow at last we would fly home to Japan. Today the three of us would each go our own way and shop to our hearts' content, but first we decided to take a commemorative photo at Monas, the National Monument.
Our lodging for two nights, Tator, included breakfast. But tomorrow we were leaving early in the morning, so today was our only chance to eat it.
A cute cat with its kitten right near the lodging.
Monas, the National Monument, towering right near Gambir Station in the city centre.
From the top of Monas we could see the plain stretching on and on, and Jakarta's high-rises nearby.
In the square below Monas there's a foot-reflexology walkway.
Yamabe and KEN first took the TransJakarta bus to a shopping centre in a busy district called Blok M.
The three of us each enjoyed shopping or a train trip.
For our last dinner in Indonesia we ate something a little luxurious. It's a Muslim country, so no toast with alcohol.
Our trip in Indonesia, packed with memories, would finally end tomorrow.
To the next day
Day 20 — Home to Japan
By DAMRI bus to Soekarno–Hatta Airport.
Farewell! Indonesia!!
On the way back we also changed in Hong Kong, and arrived at Centrair. Well done, everyone! So glad nobody got seriously hurt!
